newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian far-right stakes claim to middle ground.
newsitem.headline: Austrian far-right stakes claim to middle ground.

text.p: Freedom Party chief Joerg Haider, re-elected to head Europe's biggest far-right grouping on Saturday, sought to claim the political centre and gave a spirited defence of his party's democratic credentials.

"The Freedom Party is comparable with Germany's CSU, France's Gaullists and the liberal parties of numerous countries," Haider told a party convention in this small Alpine town 700 km (500 miles) west of Vienna and only a stone's throw from the Swiss border.

"We are nationalists. That means we want to defend our German language and national identity. We view our history with pride but we recognise its dark chapters and want to prevent a return to intolerance," he said.
Haider, Freedom Party boss since 1986, swept the leadership ballot with 98.55 percent of the vote. He was unopposed.

"Thank you very much for your confidence and I promise it will not take me another 10 years to become chancellor," he said, his voice almost drowned out by the enthusiastic cheers of the 600 delegates.
Since taking the helm the charismatic, perpetually-tanned 46-year-old has turned the Freedom Party from a marginal group with little support to the most influential far-right movement in Europe.

It scored its biggest election success to date in a European parliamentary poll on October 13, snapping at the heels of the ruling right-left coalition and picking up 27.6 percent of the vote from a public disillusioned by 21 months of EU membership.
On Saturday, the Freedom Party was at pains to rid itself of the far-right label and successive speakers accused domestic and foreign media of attacking the party unfairly.
Haider pointed to the EU candidacy of Jewish writer Peter Sichrovsky as proof of the party's liberal appeal. Sichrovsky's parents fled Austria and the Nazis during World War Two.

"In our ranks are academics, professionals and the self-employed. The future belongs to us," said Haider, who was forced to quit as provincial governor of Carinthia after praising Adolf Hitler's labour policies.

Sichrovsky told delegates the Freedom Party espoused modern liberal democratic ideas. "Liberal democracy means giving every person the same starting chance. And that is something we have lacked in Austria in recent years," said Sichrovsky, who lives in Chicago.

Susanne Riess-Passer, elected to the new post of party business manager, said the Freedom Party had no shortage of offers to team its six EU mandates with others in the Strasbourg-based European Parliament. But she too rejected links to the extreme right.
"We will choose our own allies. We do not want approaches from parties we want nothing to do with," she said.
Haider launched a fresh attack on Austria's ruling Social Democrats and their coalition partner the conservative People's and he ruled out future cooperation with either party.
"We will not cooperate with anyone who does not have the deep conviction that we are democrats," he said.
